newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to pass energy law in April to clear snags.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to pass energy law in April to clear snags.

text.p: Turkey has prepared a new law to get rid of legal obstacles to the implementation of multi-billion-dollar energy projects involving several foreign and local companies, Energy Minister Recai Kutan said on Monday.
"We have prepared the draft law and will have it passed in parliament after the upcoming (Eid al-Adha)," he told reporters on the sidelines of the "Energy Forum '97" meeting in Ankara.
"The new law will eliminate shortcomings in the model of build-operate (BO)," he said, without giving details on the law.

The model, devised by the government last year as an offshoot of its parent build-operate-transfer, will be used only for at least 13 thermal power plants worth a total of about $10 billion and with an overall capacity of 10,700 MegaWatts (MW).
The government has already tendered for six of them with a total 5,200 MW capacity and received 35 offers from 25 different companies.
"Right after the law is passed we will finalise the evaluation for the tendered power plant projects," Kutan said.
Turkey's constitutional court ruled on Thursday that the BOT model included parts violating the constitution.

The court said the BOT pattern had given the right to supervise energy projects to the government instead of the constitutional institution of the State of Council, which is the highest administrative body in Turkey.

Turkey devised the BOT model in 1984 to finance big infrastructure projects by foreign-led consortia with the government help in the procurement of inputs needed for the projects, for example oil, gas or water for power plants.
Projects under the model required examination by the Council of State and this caused delays for years for the projects to get the go-ahead.
To overcome such difficulties Turkey last year developed the build-operate (BO) model. Under the BO the inputs for power plants should be supplied by the undertakers of the project.

But the validity of both models have been challenged by many opposition MPs and pressure groups such as the Chamber of Electrical Engineers (EMO), who said the model gave concessions in the strategic product of electricity to private and foreign entities in breach of the constitution, which gives the control over such products only to the state.

Ugur Dogan, under-secretary for the energy ministry, told the meeting the new law would ensure "all the necessary legal provisions in the BO model and secure the existing tender" for the six power plants.
"We believe that we will achieve a successful result in this tender with the new law and without any delay," he said.
Kutan said the ministry asked the Council of State to speed up examinations of the joint ventures under the BOT model which can take as long as four years to finish.
Mehmet Koyunc, director of energy affairs at the ministry, told the meeting the law would eliminate all legal hindrances in the BO model.
"Despite the court ruling, the BO model will be continued to be implemented because the law will invalidate the court decision," he said.
In March the State of Council rejected an energy ministry objection to a previous decision to halt the BO system being used. The case was filed at the court by EMO against the energy ministry.

Turkey, which needs urgent energy sources and has begun importing power from Iran, Bulgaria and Georgia to close deficits this year of about 2.5 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh), tendered for six gas-fired plants, several coal-fired plants and 56 hydraulic plants under both schemes.
It also invited companies to complete the constructions of and later operate 19 hydraulic power plants under the BOT scheme.
Many international companies have bid for the projects, which has an overall cost of about $10 billion.
